We, therefore, hold that the above-mentioned 292 industries shall as per the schedule indicated hereunder change-over to the natural gas as an industrial-fuel.

claims.text: In pot-furnace units, batch preparation sieves, weighs and mixes silica sand and soda ash, and the colour and quality of the melt depend on the composition and colouring additives of the charge.

quotes.quote: (a) Batch preparation The batch charge consists of raw materials such as silica sand and soda ash. The raw material is sieved, weighed and mixed in required proportions. The composition required for pots changes depending on the requirement of color and quality of the glass.
The quality and color of melt glass in a pot is dependent on raw material composition and coloring additives in a charge batch.

claims.text: In an open pot furnace the charge is melted in pots heated to 1250-1280°C, and melting takes about 16-18 hours.

quotes.quote: (b) Melting In an open pot furnace, the charge is melted into glass in open pots placed within the furnace.
The pots filled with raw material are heated to the required temperature of 1250- 1280°C. The total time required for melting is about 16- 18 hours.

claims.text: A typical Firozabad pot furnace holds 10 to 12 pots, each charged with about 300-500 kg; the glass is melted overnight and drawn the next day.

quotes.quote: A typical pot furnace has 10 to 12 pots, with each pot holding a charge of about 300-500 kg. The pots are filled with charge material, and the glass melted overnight. The melt is drawn the following day.
The number of pots in a furnace varies between 10 and 12.
A pot furnace is a cylindrical structure, which accommodates between 10 to 12 of such pots.

claims.text: Open pots melt glass entirely for bangles, while closed or Japanese pots shield small batches of special-quality glass from furnace dust.

quotes.quote: There are two kinds of pot furnaces: open-pot and closed-pot. The closed pots (also called Japanese pots) protect the glass within the pots from
contamination by the dust and particulate matter in the furnace. Closed pots are used to melt relatively small batches of glass of special quality and composition.
Open pots are used to make glass entirely for bangles, where the quality of glass is comparatively less important.

claims.text: Each Firozabad tank furnace has a capacity to make around 15-30 tonnes of glass a day, used for items such as jars, tumblers, lamp covers, automobile headlight covers, thermos refills and laboratory ware.

quotes.quote: Tank furnaces are large: each has a capacity to make around 15-30 tonnes of glass daily. Glass from tank furnaces is used to make a wide range of items such as jars, tumblers, signal lamp covers, lamp shades, headlight covers for automobiles, thermos flasks and their refills, and laboratory ware.

claims.text: A typical pot furnace works on a downdraft principle: hot gases rise to the crown, sweep down onto the pots and leave by a flue channel below ground.

quotes.quote: furnace operates on a 'downdraft' principle, that is, the hot gases from the burning fuel flow up to the roof or crown of the furnace, and then sweep downwards on to the pots (heating them in the process) before escaping through the chimney via a flue gas channel laid beneath ground level

claims.text: Tank furnaces have brick regenerators that recover heat from flue gases to preheat combustion air, which traditional pot furnaces did not have at all.

quotes.quote: Tank furnaces are fitted with heat recovery devices called 'regenerators', which are primarily large brick structures. These devices recover heat from flue gases and use it to preheat combustion air.
pot furnaces did not have any such mechanisms at all for heat recovery.

lede.text: Firozabad Glass is the glassware of Firozabad district in Uttar Pradesh, made as glass bangles, glass beads, mouth-blown products and machine-made products.

The GI journal calls Firozabad the only place in India making glass bangles and mouth-blown glassware, though sources differ on its share of bangles, and the town is popularly known as the Glass City and as Suhag Nagri.

Glass melted in pot furnaces is drawn into a spiral on the belan and cut into raw bangles, which household workers straighten and join before the bangles are decorated and baked in the pakai bhatti, in an order sources give differently.

sentences.text: Sources differ on when glass making began at Firozabad: a District Industry Centre report traces bangle making to Jasrana sub-division in the eighteenth century, TERI places the industry's foundations in the Mughal period, and an NCDPD brochure says Firozabad has been famous for glass since the 17th century.
The GI journal recounts that Jasrana washermen found a bright glass layer on clothes warmed with local mud, which was gradually used for joint-free bangles.

The GI journal also says rejected glass articles were melted in a local furnace called Bhainsa Bhatti, so that the glass industry gradually started, and that bangles were made in the Chall Ki Bhatti by rolling glass on wooden rods.
In a story TERI tells of Akbar's reign, glass workers from Rajasthan in Firoz Shah's retinue, skilled in beads and bangles, taught their skills to local artisans.
The GI journal of 2013 lists the Japanese Pot, the Monkey Pot and the Regenerative Tank Furnace as introduced in turn, and says natural gas burners are in use in regenerative furnaces.

On 30 December 1996 the Supreme Court, as TERI puts it, banned the use of coke or coal by industries in the Taj Trapezium, and ordered 292 coal-based industries to change over to natural gas or relocate.

Sources differ on whether that order covered Firozabad: TERI says the 292 included the Firozabad pot furnace units, while the judgment confines its order to 292 industries located and operating in Agra.

Sources differ on whether coal was still burned: the GI journal says natural gas is used in place of conventional fossil fuels and Chari wrote in 2013 that most units had switched, while TERI says the pakai bhattis, not among the 292 units and excluded from GAIL's gas network, kept using coal.
In a pot-furnace bangle unit the batch of silica sand and soda ash is sieved, weighed and mixed, and melting takes about 16-18 hours.
Sources differ on the melting temperature: the DC MSME study gives 1250-1280°C for open pot furnaces, while the GI journal gives around 1450 degrees Celsius for soda lime silica glass.
A typical pot furnace holds 10 to 12 pots, and open pots melt glass entirely for bangles.
The gulliwalla scoops a glob of molten glass, which is shaped, coated with coloured block glass if necessary and reheated in the sekai bhatti.
In the belan bhatti the belanwalla turns the belan while the tarkash lays a thin glass filament on it, and the spiral is cut with a diamond cutter into rings tied in toras of about 320.
Household workers then straighten the bangles in sedhai over a small flame and join their ends in judai over a kerosene lamp.
Sources differ on the order of the last steps: TERI has the bangles decorated and then baked in the pakai bhatti, while the GI journal lists decoration with jari, ceramic work or colour after baking.
Mouth-blown flasks are blown on a hollow metal stick and shaped in dyes, while beads are drawn as hollow tubes through a dye and rounded in a revolving hot metal pipe.
The GI journal gives soda lime silica glass as 33% soda ash, 66% silica sand and 1% chemicals, and says most Firozabad products are made of it.
Borosilicate glass of 12% boron and lead glass with around 24% lead are also made.
In glassmaking generally, because silica melts at a very high temperature, soda ash and potash are added as fluxes.

In glassmaking generally, oxides of iron give a greenish-blue colour, selenium oxide red and cobalt blue, while in pot-furnace units the melt's colour depends on the colouring additives in the charge.
Selenium, an additional ingredient of red glass, is known to attack pot material faster, and one red-glass maker regained his shade in a gas-fired furnace by adding small amounts of bitumen.
Gold polish, hil, is invisible when applied and shows its lustre only when the bangles are baked.
In glassmaking generally, small amounts of potassium or sodium nitrate, arsenic oxide and antimony oxide are added to remove air bubbles from molten glass.
Soda ash and silica are the main raw materials, and bangle units also use calcium carbonate, cullet and colouring pigments.
Soda ash comes mainly from Gujarat and silica sand from Rajasthan, while chemicals and pigments are mostly imported from overseas.
The GI journal says remelted glass is a major raw material because at least half of production becomes scrap.
Broken bangles are sorted by colour in chatai and pounded into powder for the melting factory, and the 2019 study found only limited firms reusing cullet to cut raw-material costs.
TERI noted in 2008 that synthetic chemicals were then used on bangles in place of gold and silver polish.
Firozabad Glass is GI application 155 of The Glass Industries Syndicate, filed on 9 February 2009, advertised in GI Journal 54 and given certificate 202 on 31 March 2014.

Sources differ on employment: around one lakh direct workers on the GI journal's data till 2008, an estimated 150 000 direct jobs in TERI's 2008 book, nearly 5-6 lakh in a 2011 seminar brochure and more than 5 lakh in the 2019 DC MSME study.

Sources differ on turnover and exports: around Rs 800 crore with Rs 62.2 crore exported on the GI journal's data till 2008; more than Rs 2000 crore in 2011, when a seminar brochure put exports at around 50% of small-scale units' produce; and nearly 35% exported in the 2019 DC MSME study, over INR 278 crore in 2017-18.

The GI journal of 2013 counts 421 registered glassware manufacturing units, 47 of them exporting, while the 2019 DC MSME study counts close to 198 registered manufacturing firms besides 4000-5000 household units.
Sources differ on Firozabad's share of India's bangles: about 90% (Chari, 2013), almost the entire demand (TERI, 2008), the entire requirement (NCDPD, 2011) and an absolute monopoly (GI journal).
The 2019 DC MSME study counts about 130-140 pot-furnace units, while its cluster table gives 115-120 bangle units.
Household bangle workers are paid piece-rate wages through contractors called thekedars, and in mid-2007 they got 9 rupees per tora for sedhai and judai.
The 2019 study costs one toda of 320 bangles at INR 125 to produce, with a selling price of 137.5.
A 2014 study found the lung function of 100 Firozabad bangle workers significantly reduced, with impairment rising with years of exposure to smoke and flue.
A study published in 1987 found severe heat stress on workers in eight bangle units, and a study of 19 boys in one bangle factory found cardio-respiratory strain from heat.
Baseline studies in 2002/03 found household bangle workers, mainly women and children, exposed to very high pollution at home, and decorators using corrosive acids and other toxic chemicals.
TERI reported in 2008 that children continued to work in household bangle making despite the 1986 Child Labour Act.
The 2019 study found workers exposed to high temperatures, flue gases and fumes, using little safety equipment and facing the threat of silicosis.
Down To Earth reports that the dyes used to colour bangle glass contain lead, cadmium and mercury.
The GI area is Firozabad district, with glassware making confined to in and around Firozabad town and a few nearby places.
The GI application names Agra Road, Station Road, Coal siding, Ashafabagh, Makkanpur, Dholpura and Raja ka Taal as the epicentre of glassware making in and around Firozabad town.
Sources place Firozabad 40 km from Agra and about 240 or 250 km from Delhi.
Firozabad district was formed in February 1989 from areas of Agra and Mainpuri districts.
A huge area of Firozabad lies in the Taj Trapezium Zone of 10,400 sq km around the Taj Mahal.
The GI journal says bangles are coloured with coloured glass or with colour applied to the upper crest, and a colour layer called batti can be sandwiched between transparent layers.
A bangle can be round, flat, oval or spiral depending on how the loam is beaten, and the GI journal specifies four standard sizes, S, M, L and XL.
A kada is a thick bangle made by melting several bangles together, with designs drawn on it with a thin glass stick.
Bangles are closely associated with marriage, or suhag, and the GI journal says joint-free Kadechhal Ki Choori, made at Sasani near Aligarh, are considered very auspicious for the bride.
Sources differ on how many hands a bangle passes through: 54 in the GI journal, 50 in a popular saying and 139 in a 1997 estimate.
A typical pot furnace works on a downdraft principle, with hot gases sweeping down from the crown onto the pots.
Tank furnaces recover heat from flue gases in brick regenerators, which traditional pot furnaces did not have.

Without thermocouples, firemen of traditional coal-fired pot furnaces judged temperature by the colour of the furnace interior, from initial red at 500-550 °C to full white at 1500 °C on TERI's rough guide.
Annealing heats and cools glass in a controlled way to remove strains, and flasks cool gradually in a temperature-controlled chamber called the Layer.
